Why is Modi telling us to save when economy’s robust? GDP growth story hides cautious household subplot

If Milton Friedman’s permanent income hypothesis is considered, true assessment for this quarter was not provided by MoSPI. This was determined by approach of cautious households.

Bidisha Bhattacharya

02 September, 2026 10:22 pm IST

The Indian economy is expanding faster than consumer spending, and the divergence between these two metrics is critical in determining whether an investment-led boom is sustainable or vulnerable | Reuters File

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: On Tuesday, during a speech in Bishkek, the Prime Minister lauded the country’s 7.8% economic growth, the highest rate among major global economies, while simultaneously urging Indian citizens to reduce their gold purchases.

This juxtaposition raises questions about why an economy experiencing such robust growth would require its citizens to prioritise saving over spending. This apparent contradiction is not merely a minor detail in the current GDP release; it is the release itself.

Beneath the headline figure, two key indicators, namely, household spending and gold purchases, are both experiencing a subtle decline. These trends, which the 7.8% growth figure does not capture, reflect the actual sentiments of ordinary households regarding the future. This story contrasts with the optimistic portrayal presented on the day of the GDP release, highlighting a more nuanced story that merits attention.

Show Full Article

Momentum, measured against itself In the first quarter of the fiscal year 2027, real GDP increased by 7.8%, compared to a growth rate of 6.9% in the corresponding period of the previous year. This comparison is noteworthy.

Gfx: ThePrint | Credit: MoSPI In three of the last four quarters, growth rates have been recorded at or above 7.8%, with the peak reaching 8.6% in Q4 FY26, immediately preceding the current quarter.

This reflects a deceleration from a high base rather than a new acceleration, and confusing the two is a common error in growth reporting. Additionally, this is only the second quarterly report under India’s new 2022-23 base year, which replaced the decade-old 2011-12 series in February and incorporated double deflation for manufacturing.

This change constitutes a significant methodological enhancement in accordance with the UN System of National Accounts. Historical base-year revisions in India have yielded mixed outcomes, as exemplified by the 2015 revision, which adjusted the economy’s absolute size downward while growth rates increased for several years.

The current revision shows a similarly uneven pattern, with growth for one recent year revised downward and another upward, depending on the year examined. This does not render the 7.8% figure inaccurate; rather, it indicates that the measurement is based on a newly established benchmark, the full implications of which are yet to be fully understood.

Growth without the growers The composition of the 7.8% growth becomes more significant than its magnitude when each sector’s growth is weighted according to its actual contribution to the economy. This approach, rather than considering growth rates in isolation, identifies the quarter’s actual sources of growth.

Gfx: ThePrint | Credit: Bidisha Bhattacharya The tertiary sector—encompassing financial services, IT, real estate, and professional services—accounted for 4.92 of the 7.8 percentage points, representing 63% of the total contribution.

The secondary sector contributed an additional 1.99 points, while the primary sector added only 0.53 points. This sub-sector includes a wide range of activities, from bank lending and capital markets to imputed rent on owner-occupied homes, suggesting it is not solely a corporate phenomenon.

The magnitude and composition allow it to influence the overall headline figure without necessitating a corresponding increase in typical household expenditure. The subsequent expenditure-side data corroborate this observation.

The consumer who isn’t keeping pace Private Final Consumption Expenditure, which represents the actual spending by ordinary households, increased by 7.1% in real terms this quarter. This growth rate is lower than the 7.8% GDP figure and significantly lags behind the 11.9% growth rate of investment.

An examination of the current-price data reveals an even wider gap: the share of household consumption in GDP decreased from 55.8% to 55.6% year-on-year. Although this change appears minor, it carries significant implications. The Indian economy is expanding faster than consumer spending, and the divergence between these two metrics is critical in determining whether an investment-led boom is sustainable or vulnerable.

The mechanism likely influencing this scenario is best understood through explanation rather than mere citation.

American economist Milton Friedman’s permanent income hypothesis posits that households base their spending not on current income but on anticipated long-term income.

When these expectations become uncertain because of factors such as disruptions in energy markets caused by war, currency instability, or a base-year revision that lacks widespread trust, households tend to reduce spending pre-emptively.

This behaviour, known as precautionary saving, helps explain why an economy can report impressive investment figures and only moderate consumption growth in the same quarter. Investment reflects optimism of firms and governments about future prospects, whereas consumption reflects households’ perceptions of future security. Currently, these perspectives are misaligned.

Gold is telling the same story, more loudly During this quarter, the mining sector experienced a contraction of 2.4%, distinguishing it as the sole sub-sector to decline, despite a 58% increase in the prices of crude oil and natural gas. This scenario, characterised by reduced output and increased prices, is indicative of a supply shock rather than diminished demand, and is directly linked to the disruptions in West Asia that are influencing household expectations.

Gfx: ThePrint | Credit: MoSPI This context forms the backdrop for the Prime Minister’s appeal, his second this year, urging the conservation of foreign exchange amidst a widening trade deficit.

The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) provides data that allows an evaluation of the appeal’s effectiveness, revealing insights that are more pronounced than they initially appear.

The GDP category labelled as Valuables, which includes gold and jewellery purchased as a store of value, contracted by 18.6% in real terms this quarter, continuing a significant decline from the previous year. In nominal terms, however, this category grew by 33.4%, solely due to a rally in global gold prices.

When the price effect is excluded, it becomes evident that Indians purchased significantly less gold. Conversely, including the price effect suggests a surge in gold purchases. This reflects a shift in precautionary saving behaviour: in times of uncertainty, households do not cease saving but alter its form.

The reduction in gold purchases may not necessarily reflect a patriotic response to the PM’s appeal; it could equally be attributed to the nearly 10% increase in gold prices within a single month, which may have priced marginal buyers out of the market.

It is plausible that both moral suasion and price dynamics are influencing behaviour, and determining the precise contribution of each factor is complex and requires further investigation rather than premature conclusions.

It is important to acknowledge that broader customs data on gold imports during the same period indicate an opposite trend, highlighting that the household-level valuables category and aggregate trade figures measure different aspects. This unresolved tension is an integral part of the narrative.

What next two quarters owe us The 7.8% figure is not erroneous; it is incomplete. This incompleteness is characterised by a growth engine driven predominantly by a single sector that only partially affects household life, an investment surge that exceeds the consumer spending needed to justify it, and a gold market where price and quantity diverge for the same fundamental reason.

Friedman’s hypothesis says that consumption is influenced not by current income, but by confidence in future income. According to this perspective, the true assessment for this quarter was not provided by the MoSPI.

Instead, it was determined by numerous households opting to adopt a cautious approach. This decision will not be reflected in a single statistic until the subsequent two data releases, scheduled for November and February, indicate whether this period of caution concludes with relief or presents further challenges.

(Edited by Tony Rai)
